intro: Correlated feature directions can duplicate information. A Gram-matrix penalty encourages columns to have unit norm and be mutually orthogonal.
task: Return the squared Frobenius penalty on W.T@W-I and its gradient with respect to W.
requirements: weights is a rows-by-columns matrix. Define G=W.T@W-I with an identity sized by the number of columns.
Return {"loss": sum(G*G), "gradient": 4*W@G}. Do not average the loss or divide by batch size. More columns than rows is allowed, although zero loss is then impossible.

Use finite real numeric values of magnitude at most 1e6, excluding boolean inputs. Each array axis has 1..64 entries and at most 65536 elements total unless a stricter bound is stated. Return NumPy arrays for array outputs, preserve caller inputs, and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

examples.name: Already orthogonal
examples.output:
{'loss': 0.0, 'gradient': [[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

examples.name: Scaled axes
examples.output:
{'loss': 9.0, 'gradient': [[24.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

examples.name: Correlated columns
examples.output:
{'loss': 2.0, 'gradient': [[4.0, 4.0], [0.0, 0.0]]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

hints.title: Follow the data
hints.body: The diagonal of the Gram matrix measures squared column norms; off-diagonal entries measure inner products.

hints.title: Check the boundary
hints.body: The derivative receives equal contributions from both appearances of W.

explanation: The penalty treats unit length and independence as one matrix objective. Its gradient moves columns in response to both their norms and their pairwise correlations.
When columns outnumber the ambient dimension, they cannot all be orthonormal. The function still provides a well-defined optimization objective rather than rejecting the rectangular matrix.
